findings.title: Secret-scan scope: verified credentials only, and history is not pattern-scanned
findings.evidence: TruffleHog runs with --only-verified on all three passes (source tree, git history, built bundle): a credential it detects but cannot verify against the live provider is not reported. gitleaks runs alongside with --no-git, so its pattern pass covers the WORKING TREE only and never walks git history.
findings.impact: A credential that exists only in git history AND cannot be verified — already rotated or expired, an internal/custom provider TruffleHog has no verifier for, or any provider unreachable from the scanning host — falls between the two tools and is not covered. Working-tree secrets are covered by both tools; this gap is specific to history.
findings.fix: To close it for this engagement, run `trufflehog git --results=unverified --json file://<repo>` against the client repository from a host with outbound network access and triage the unverified hits by hand.

findings.title: brace-expansion@1.1.16: brace-expansion: DoS via unbounded expansion length causing an out-of-memory process crash (fixed in 5.0.8 / 3.0.3 / 2.1.3 / 1.1.17)
findings.evidence: OSV-Scanner matched GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg (aliases: CVE-2026-14257) against brace-expansion@1.1.16. Rated High from the advisory's own HIGH rating. The advisory's affected range is fixed in 5.0.8 / 3.0.3 / 2.1.3 / 1.1.17. Advisory: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-14257.
findings.impact:
brace-expansion: DoS via unbounded expansion length causing an out-of-memory process crash — `expand()` bounds the *number* of results it produces (the `max` option,
`100_000` by default) but not their *length*. By chaining many brace groups,
an attacker keeps the result count under `max` while making every result grow
with the number of groups. Building `max` long results — plus the intermediate
arrays combined at each brace group — exhausts memory and crashes the Node
process with an **uncatchable** out-of-memory error. `try/catch` around
`expand()` does not help: the fatal error terminates the process.
findings.fix: Upgrade brace-expansion to 5.0.8 or later (see GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg).
cwe: CWE-400
CWE-770

reachability.justification: brace-expansion is not a direct dependency and no scanned source file imports it — it is pulled in by another package. Your own code does not call it directly, but the package that does may. De-prioritizes the row, does not clear it.

findings.evidence: OSV-Scanner matched GHSA-rgw5-rvv9-x895 (aliases: CVE-2026-69152) against brace-expansion@1.1.16. Rated High from the advisory's own HIGH rating. The advisory's affected range is fixed in 1.1.18 / 2.1.4 / 3.0.6 / 5.0.9. Advisory: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69152.

A ~25 KB input still crashes the Node process with an **uncatchable** out-of-memory error, so `try/catch` around `expand()` does not help.

findings.title: braces@2.3.2: Uncontrolled resource consumption in braces (fixed in 3.0.3)
findings.evidence: OSV-Scanner matched GHSA-grv7-fg5c-xmjg (aliases: CVE-2024-4068) against braces@2.3.2. Rated High from the advisory's own HIGH rating. The advisory's affected range is fixed in 3.0.3. Advisory: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-4068.
findings.impact: Uncontrolled resource consumption in braces — The NPM package `braces` fails to limit the number of characters it can handle, which could lead to Memory Exhaustion. In `lib/parse.js,` if a malicious user sends "imbalanced braces" as input, the parsing will enter a loop, which will cause the program to start allocating heap memory without freeing it at any moment of the loop. Eventually, the JavaScript heap limit is reached, and the program will crash.
findings.fix: Upgrade braces to 3.0.3 or later (see GHSA-grv7-fg5c-xmjg).
cwe: CWE-400

findings.evidence: OSV-Scanner matched GHSA-4mjr-xmp4-gh2g (aliases: CVE-2026-82417) against qs@6.15.3. Rated Medium from the advisory's own MODERATE rating. The advisory's affected range is fixed in 6.16.0. Advisory: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-82417.
findings.impact: qs: Denial of Service via Attacker Controlled isBuffer — `qs.stringify()` calls `utils.isBuffer()` on every value it serializes, and `utils.isBuffer()` invokes `obj.constructor.isBuffer(obj)` without checking that it is callable. A value whose own `constructor.isBuffer` is a non-function makes `qs` call a non-callable and throw `TypeError`. Such a value is produced **by `qs.parse` itself** from an untrusted query string when `plainObjects: true` or `allowPrototypes: true` is set, so a pure-`qs` `parse` → `stringify` round-trip — no `JSON.parse` — turns an unauthenticated query string into an uncaught throw.
findings.fix: Upgrade qs to 6.16.0 or later (see GHSA-4mjr-xmp4-gh2g).

findings.title: javascript.node-crypto.security.create-de-cipher-no-iv.create-de-cipher-no-iv: The deprecated functions 'createCipher' and 'createDecipher' generate the same initialization vector every time. For counter modes such as CTR, GCM, or CCM this leads to break of both confidentiality and integrity, if the key is used more than once. findings.title: javascript.node-crypto.security.gcm-no-tag-length.gcm-no-tag-length: The call to 'createDecipheriv' with the Galois Counter Mode (GCM) mode of operation is missing an expected authentication tag length. If the expected authentication tag length is not specified or otherwise checked, the application might be tricked into verifying a shorter-than-expected authentication tag. This can be abused by an attacker to spoof ciphertexts or recover the implicit authentication key of GCM, allowing arbitrary forgeries.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-argument-injection: Request input is passed as an argv-array element to execFile/spawn (no shell) — argument injection (CWE-88). Even without a shell, a leading -/--flag value is interpreted as an option by the invoked program. Validate the value against an allowlist and pass `--` before positional arguments. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK (#1342), so its silence elsewhere is not read as a clean bill of health: it reports the tainted argv element. Whether that is exploitable depends on how the invoked program treats a leading dash — a binary with no option parsing, or one already given `--`, is not at risk — and no source scan can determine that.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-auth-admin-in-client: supabase.auth.admin.* (the service-role-only GoTrue admin API) is called inside a Client Component ("use client") on what looks like the service-role client. The privileged admin client ships to the browser. Move all auth.admin usage into a server-only route/action. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK: it keys off the client's BINDING NAME (one reading as admin/service), because there is no cross-file taint here — an admin client bound to a name that does not read that way is not assessed.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-authed-no-role-check: This admin/privileged route establishes a session (Supabase getUser/getSession or a custom jwt.verify/verifyToken/requireAuth) but performs no role/permission check before returning privileged data — broken function-level authorization (OWASP API5). It correctly rejects anonymous callers, but any authenticated lower-privilege user (e.g. a member) reaches it. Add a server-side role/permission gate after authenticating. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK: it reads only files whose path contains admin/internal/privileged — a privileged handler on any other path is not assessed — and it is a review-tier signal, so a role gate expressed in a form this rule does not recognise reads here as missing.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-client-trusted-price: A price, discount or trial length is read directly from a client-supplied request field. If it reaches a charge, subscription or entitlement write, any caller can set their own price or extend their own trial by adding the field to the request. Re-read the value server-side from the price/plan record identified by the request, never from the request body itself. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK (#1373), so its silence elsewhere is not read as a clean bill of health: it reports the READ of a named money/trial field off the request and does not trace it to a payment sink, so a handler that reads the field only to compare or reject it appears here too. It matches a fixed field vocabulary, so a codebase using other names for the same values is not assessed; bare `amount`, `total` and `quantity` are deliberately outside that vocabulary because they carry too many benign meanings to name without a payment-sink gate.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-cookie-insecure: Set-Cookie is written with no Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite attributes. A session cookie without HttpOnly is readable by any injected script (XSS → session theft); without Secure it can be sent over plain HTTP; without SameSite it rides cross-site requests. The `(?s)^[^;]*$` match below proves the cookie carries no attribute at all, so all three weaknesses are determined by the same evidence and this finding names all three.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-csv-formula-injection-client-url: A client URL parameter is serialized by PapaParse or SheetJS into a CSV/spreadsheet export without neutralizing formula prefixes. Node-only CSV serializers are outside this client-source rule and remain covered by the request-source companion.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-csv-formula-injection: Request input is serialized into a CSV/spreadsheet export without neutralizing formula prefixes — CSV formula injection. A cell starting `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, tab or CR is executed as a formula by Excel and Google Sheets when a colleague opens the export, which is enough to exfiltrate the sheet to an attacker-controlled URL. Prefix such cells with a single quote or reject them at write time. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK, both halves MEASURED 2026-07-31 against planted shapes. (1) It is taint-gated on a REQUEST source, so it reports the reflected variant — input that reaches the exporter in the same request. The commoner STORED variant, where a value is written to the database in one request and exported in another, crosses a persistence boundary this rule does not follow and is NOT reported by it. (2) It matches the CSV/spreadsheet SERIALIZERS (csv-stringify, fast-csv, papaparse, json2csv, SheetJS) AT THEIR CONVENTIONAL MODULE BINDINGS — the bare `stringify`/`writeToString` arms require the file to import one of those modules (either `import` or `require`), and the json2csv arm requires both a json2csv import and its own exported constructor name. A serializer reached through a re-export, an export wrapper or an unconventional alias is NOT matched, and neither is a CSV assembled by string concatenation and handed to `res.send`. Read its silence accordingly.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-dangerously-set-inner-html-prop: A prop/parameter/identifier value reaches dangerouslySetInnerHTML with no sanitizer. If any of the data on this path is user-controlled (a bio, a comment, markdown, an AI-generated string), this is stored/reflected XSS. Sanitize with DOMPurify.sanitize before it reaches __html, or render the value as text. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK (#1342), so its silence elsewhere is not read as a clean bill of health: it reports the prop or identifier reaching __html. Whether the value was already sanitized upstream — by the component's caller, a shared formatter, or at write time — is outside what this rule reads, so a correctly sanitized value can still appear here.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-jsx-prop-spread-injection: An attacker-controlled object is spread into a component's props — the caller chooses which props the component receives, including dangerouslySetInnerHTML, so this is an XSS sink that never names one. Filter the object against an explicit allowlist of prop names before spreading it, and never use a blocklist (new dangerous props keep being added). SCOPE OF THIS CHECK (#1342/#1237), so its silence elsewhere is not read as a clean bill of health: a spread object is treated as safe only when it passes an explicit allowlist test in one of three recognised spellings — Object.fromEntries over a .has/.includes filter, pick(), or a for-of copy whose keys come from a NAMED allowlist (for (const k of ALLOWED) safe[k] = raw[k]). Any other sanitizer — a custom filter function, a validation library, a schema parse — is not recognised, so a correctly filtered spread can still be reported here. The recognised test is a structural match on the filtering code, not evidence that the allowlist it uses is itself complete: MEASURED 2026-07-31, a loop whose allowlist is laundered through a local const off the untrusted object (const allowed = raw.fields; for (const k of allowed) ...) is NOT reported, the same one-hop indirection the .has/.includes arm has always had.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-jwt-decode-noverify: jwt.decode() reads the token's claims WITHOUT verifying the signature. If the result feeds an authorization decision, anyone can forge a token with an arbitrary claim (no key needed). Use jwt.verify() (with an explicit algorithms allowlist) for anything security-relevant. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK (#1342), so its silence elsewhere is not read as a clean bill of health: it flags EVERY jwt.decode() call. Telling a decode that feeds an authorization decision from one that only reads a claim for display or refresh timing needs the caller's control flow, which this rule does not follow — so an informational decode is expected to appear here and is not, on its own, a defect.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-ldap-injection: Request input reaches an LDAP search filter or bind DN unescaped — LDAP injection. `*)(uid=*` rewrites the filter into one that matches every entry, and in an LDAP-backed login that is an authentication bypass. findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-open-redirect: Redirect target derives from a request-controlled value with no host allowlist — a classic open-redirect primitive for phishing (and SSRF-shaped if fetched server-side). SCOPE OF THIS CHECK (#1342), so its silence elsewhere is not read as a clean bill of health: it follows the value within this file only. A host allowlist enforced elsewhere — in shared middleware, a route wrapper, or a helper the value passes through — is not something this rule reads, so confirm no such guard runs before treating this as unmitigated. A host allowlist that rejects by THROWING is recognised (#1248) only when no `try` follows the `new URL(...)` projection in the same scope, so a correct guard whose URL parse is itself wrapped in try/catch is reported here rather than cleared.

Silence on either omitted shape is not an assessment of it.

findings.title: src.scan.rules.semgrep.harvey-xxe-parse: Request-controlled input is parsed as XML through an XXE-capable parser (libxmljs/DOMParser). If external-entity resolution is enabled, this is XXE (file read / SSRF via DOCTYPE entities). Disable entity resolution (e.g. libxmljs { noent: false }) and validate the input. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK (#1342), so its silence elsewhere is not read as a clean bill of health: it reports the parse of request-controlled XML, NOT proof that external-entity resolution is enabled. Whether it is depends on parser options that may be set in config this rule does not read, so exploitability has to be confirmed against the parser's actual settings. Two XML parsers are DELIBERATELY not matched (#1273) and their absence is not a gap: `sax` resolves no DTD entities at all (its README: "It's possible to define additional entities in XML by putting them in the DTD. This parser doesn't do anything with that"), and `node-expat` exposes no external-entity handler, so neither reaches an external entity. Feed either one XML you do not trust and you still own a resource-exhaustion question, which is a different weakness from this one and is not what this rule reports. Browser-native DOMParser fed from a client URL parameter is ALSO deliberately excluded (#1708): current stable browser engines do not fetch or expand an external DTD through DOMParser.parseFromString, so that client-local parse is outside this XXE threat model. Server-side DOMParser polyfills and libxmljs remain in scope when fed from a request source.

findings.title: yaml.github-actions.security.pull-request-target-code-checkout.pull-request-target-code-checkout: This GitHub Actions workflow file uses `pull_request_target` and checks out code from the incoming pull request. When using `pull_request_target`, the Action runs in the context of the target repository, which includes access to all repository secrets. Normally, this is safe because the Action only runs code from the target repository, not the incoming PR. However, by checking out the incoming PR code, you're now using the incoming code for the rest of the action. You may be inadvertently executing arbitrary code from the incoming PR with access to repository secrets, which would let an attacker steal repository secrets. This normally happens by running build scripts (e.g., `npm build` and `make`) or dependency installation scripts (e.g., `python setup.py install`). Audit your workflow file to make sure no code from the incoming PR is executed. Please see https://securitylab.github.com/research/github-actions-preventing-pwn-requests/ for additional mitigations.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy configured
findings.evidence: No Content-Security-Policy found in next.config.js, middleware.ts.
findings.impact: No CSP leaves XSS sinks (e.g. dangerouslySetInnerHTML) without a defense-in-depth mitigation.
findings.fix: Add a Content-Security-Policy header (in next.config headers(), middleware, or the hosting platform config).
cwe: CWE-693: Protection Mechanism Failure

findings.title: Hosting config sets response headers but not Strict-Transport-Security
findings.evidence: No Strict-Transport-Security found in the hosting header config (public/_headers).
findings.impact: Without HSTS a user's first request (or any downgraded request) can be intercepted over plain HTTP before the redirect to HTTPS.
findings.fix: Add a Strict-Transport-Security header (e.g. `max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains`) in the hosting config.
cwe: CWE-693: Protection Mechanism Failure

findings.title: Hosting config sets response headers but not X-Frame-Options
findings.evidence: No X-Frame-Options found in the hosting header config (public/_headers).
findings.impact: Without X-Frame-Options (or a CSP frame-ancestors directive) the page can be framed by any site and used for clickjacking.
findings.fix: Add `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or a CSP `frame-ancestors 'none'` directive) in the hosting config.
cwe: CWE-693: Protection Mechanism Failure

findings.title: Hosting config sets response headers but not X-Content-Type-Options
findings.evidence: No X-Content-Type-Options found in the hosting header config (public/_headers).
findings.impact: Without X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff a browser may MIME-sniff a response into an executable content type.
findings.fix: Add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` in the hosting config.

findings.title: public.billing_exports has row level security turned back OFF by a later migration
findings.taxonomy: Migration disables RLS on a public table (static)
findings.evidence: "alter table public.billing_exports disable row level security" in supabase/migrations/20260728000003_rls_disable_hotfix.sql is the LAST row-security statement for this table across the migration set, so the table ships with RLS off no matter how many earlier migrations enabled it.
findings.impact: A public-schema table with RLS off is auto-exposed via PostgREST — every row is readable/writable by anyone holding the anon key. Any policies still defined on the table are inert: Postgres does not consult them while row security is disabled, so the schema reads as protected and behaves as public.
findings.fix: Remove the disable statement, or follow it with "alter table public.billing_exports enable row level security;" in the same migration if it was only needed for a backfill.
cwe: CWE-862: Missing Authorization

findings.title: Role mt_app_worker is granted BYPASSRLS, which voids every row-level policy for that role
findings.taxonomy: Role with BYPASSRLS defeats row-level security (static)
findings.evidence: create role mt_app_worker login bypassrls — in supabase/migrations/20260726000002_owasp_mt_isolation.sql.
findings.impact: PostgreSQL documents that roles with BYPASSRLS always bypass row security; FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY does not constrain them, because FORCE governs the table owner. Any request served over a connection using this role reads and writes every tenant's rows regardless of the policies defined on the table.
findings.fix: Remove BYPASSRLS from mt_app_worker (`alter role mt_app_worker nobypassrls;`) and reserve privileged connections for migrations and administrative jobs. If a code path must use one to serve user requests, it has to re-implement tenant scoping itself, because the database will no longer do it.
cwe: CWE-269: Improper Privilege Management

findings.title: 31 RLS-enabled table(s) never force row level security, so the owning role bypasses their policies
findings.taxonomy: RLS enabled without FORCE — owner bypasses policies (static)
findings.evidence: 31 table(s) have "enable row level security" and at least one policy but no matching "force row level security" in any migration: audit_events, billing_prices, billing_products, billing_profiles, billing_subscriptions, compliance_case_notes_archived, counters, device_pings, documents, gadgets, import_staging, internal_notes, invoices, mt_ledger, newsletter_subscribers, nocode_invoices, notes, patient_billing, perf_events, perf_line_items, perf_orders, perf_shipments, pii_calibration_fixture, plans, profiles, support_categories, support_tickets, tautology_articles, tenant_reports, tenants, widgets. Review question: Does any runtime code path connect as the role that OWNS these tables? On a stock Supabase project PostgREST connects as anon/authenticated, which are not the owner, and this is defence-in-depth only. A self-hosted or custom-pooled deployment that connects as the owning role has no row-level isolation on these tables at all.
findings.impact: PostgreSQL exempts a table's owner from row security unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set. Where the owning role is used at runtime, every policy listed here holds for non-owner roles only.
findings.fix: Add `alter table public.<table> force row level security;` alongside each enable statement — inert when the owner never serves requests, and closes the gap when it does.
findings.okWhen: Runtime access is exclusively through PostgREST as anon/authenticated, or through a role that does not own these tables — the stock hosted-Supabase arrangement. FORCE is then hardening, not a fix.
findings.notOkWhen: Any application connection, pooler, migration job or edge function connects as the table-owning role (common in self-hosted deployments and in direct-Postgres access alongside PostgREST) — those paths read and write every tenant's rows.
cwe: CWE-269: Improper Privilege Management

findings.title: RLS on public.device_pings grants the client a write policy but no SELECT policy
findings.taxonomy: RLS policy set grants a write with no read policy (static permission matrix)
findings.evidence: Command x role for public.device_pings, read from the live policy set at the end of migration history: INSERT (to authenticated); UPDATE (to authenticated); DELETE (to authenticated) — no policy for SELECT. SCOPE OF THIS RULE: only a table that grants a WRITE command with no SELECT policy is reported. A table whose uncovered commands are writes only — read policed, writes server-side — is the standard Supabase arrangement and is not reported; 23 table(s) in this schema are in that state. Review question: Which connection READS public.device_pings? The policy set lets the client write rows it has no policy to select, so either a read policy is missing by oversight, or reads run over a service-role connection, a SECURITY DEFINER function or the table owner — and that path's tenant scoping is application code this RLS pass does not read.
findings.impact: Row security denies a command outright when no policy grants it, so the uncovered SELECT is not an exposure in itself — the rows are unreadable through PostgREST. The exposure question is the read path that must exist somewhere else: a service-role client returns every tenant's rows unless the application filters them, and nothing in these migrations says whether it does.
findings.fix: Add the SELECT policy if the client is meant to read these rows back (scoped the same way the write policies are), or record that reads are deliberately server-only and confirm the code performing them scopes rows to the caller's tenant itself.
findings.okWhen: The client genuinely never reads this table — an append-only event or audit sink whose reads happen in server code that filters by tenant — and that filtering has been reviewed.
findings.notOkWhen: A user-facing route reads this table through the service-role key, or through a SECURITY DEFINER function with no caller check: those rows are not covered by any policy above, and whatever scopes them to one tenant is unreviewed by this pass.
cwe: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control

findings.title: RLS policy public.profiles.profiles_select_self — semantic tenancy review
findings.evidence: Policy scopes by a caller-identity function but never references the tenant key "tenant_id" — it may isolate on the wrong column (per-user where per-tenant is required, or vice-versa). Live clauses — SELECT USING: id = auth.uid(); WITH CHECK: (none). Review question: Does this policy restrict every row it exposes/accepts to the caller's own tenant under the declared tenancy model (tenant key "tenant_id")?
findings.impact: A policy that keys on the wrong column or under-constrains writes lets one tenant read or write another tenant's rows even though RLS is enabled.
findings.fix: Compare the tenant key "tenant_id" against the caller's verified tenant (e.g. a JWT claim) in both USING and WITH CHECK, and make WITH CHECK at least as strict as USING.
findings.okWhen: The policy already constrains every exposed/accepted row to the caller's own tenant, and the column it keys on is genuinely the tenant boundary.
findings.notOkWhen: The policy keys on a non-tenant column, or its WITH CHECK is weaker than its USING, so cross-tenant reads or writes slip through.

Live clauses — SELECT USING: true; WITH CHECK: (none). Review question: Does this policy restrict every row it exposes/accepts to the caller's own tenant under the declared tenancy model (tenant key "tenant_id")?
findings.impact: A policy that keys on the wrong column or under-constrains writes lets one tenant read or write another tenant's rows even though RLS is enabled.
findings.fix: Compare the tenant key "tenant_id" against the caller's verified tenant (e.g. a JWT claim) in both USING and WITH CHECK, and make WITH CHECK at least as strict as USING.
findings.okWhen: The policy already constrains every exposed/accepted row to the caller's own tenant, and the column it keys on is genuinely the tenant boundary.
findings.notOkWhen: The policy keys on a non-tenant column, or its WITH CHECK is weaker than its USING, so cross-tenant reads or writes slip through.

findings.title: World-readable policy on newsletter_subscribers, which M10 classified as holding personal data
findings.taxonomy: USING(true) read policy on an M10-classified PII table (static)
findings.evidence: Policy newsletter_subscribers_select_all on public.newsletter_subscribers read with USING (true), so every row is in scope for every caller the policy applies to — including anon, unless a role restriction narrows it. The table declares no recognised tenant key, which normally leaves this shape SPARED as an unassessed catalog; M10's classification of the same migration SQL says it is not a catalog: email (EMAIL) (PII, data score 1).
findings.impact: Every row of newsletter_subscribers — including email for every user — is readable by anyone the policy admits. This is the shape that reads as "no findings" when the two signals are looked at separately: the policy review spares it for want of a tenant key, and the data map records the columns without knowing who can read them.
findings.fix: Confirm public.newsletter_subscribers is genuinely meant to be world-readable. If it is not, replace USING (true) with an owner or tenant predicate (e.g. USING (id = auth.uid()) for a per-user table), and re-run with `--tenant-key <column>` if the table is tenant-scoped under a name the review does not recognise.
cwe: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

findings.title: Tenancy model assumed by the static RLS review
findings.evidence: The static policy review inferred tenancy PER TABLE by looking for one of the known tenant-key columns (tenant_id, org_id, organization_id, workspace_id, account_id, company_id). Reviewed as per-tenant: profiles → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; notes → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; counters → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; documents → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; invoices → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; pii_calibration_fixture → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; perf_orders → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; perf_events → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; internal_notes → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; support_tickets → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; tenant_reports → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; tautology_articles → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; audit_events → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; patient_billing → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; mt_ledger → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; mt_contracts → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; d091_quotes → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; d091_bookings → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; d091_contacts → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; d091_contacts_unique → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; d091_contacts_readonly → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; job_queue → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; rollup_daily → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; billing_exports → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; import_staging → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; device_pings → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; compliance_case_notes_archived → per-tenant on "tenant_id"; nocode_invoices → per-tenant on "tenant_id". Reviewed as per-user (no recognised tenant column — a row bound to auth.uid() is treated as the isolation boundary): tenants, perf_line_items, perf_shipments, objects, plans, widgets, gadgets, newsletter_subscribers, support_categories, billing_products, billing_prices, billing_subscriptions, billing_profiles. NOT RECOGNISED — these tables declare a scoping column that is not on the known list, so they were reviewed as per-user and any cross-tenant policy bug in them WAS NOT LOOKED FOR: perf_line_items (declares order_id); perf_shipments (declares order_id); widgets (declares site); billing_prices (declares product_id). Coverage note: the scoping-column scan above names a column when it ends in "_id" OR is a foreign key to a tenant-shaped table (tenants/orgs/accounts/workspaces/companies). A bare tenant column with NEITHER signal — an off-list name (e.g. "tenant", "site", "region_slug") and no FK to a tenant table — is still reviewed as per-user and will not be named. An empty list above is not proof that no such column exists.
findings.impact: This is the review's central assumption, not a defect. If a table listed as per-user is really tenant-scoped under a name the list does not know (e.g. site_id), its policies were judged against the wrong model and cross-tenant findings were silently missed — a failed inference is indistinguishable from a clean result unless it is stated.
findings.fix: Confirm the assumed model above. If a table is tenant-scoped under a column not listed, re-run this scan with `--tenant-key <column>` (quick-scan / mechanical scan, or detect-deeper at the connected tier) — the reviewer uses the declared column for any table that has it instead of guessing from the built-in list. Use `--tenant-mode per-user` instead if the app is genuinely single-tenant end to end. Until re-run, treat the per-user verdict for any unlisted table as not assessed.

findings.title: USING (true) policies left unassessed — no recognised tenant key to judge them against
findings.evidence: These policies open every row of their table (USING is "true") on a table that declares no recognised tenant key, so the tenant-scoped USING(true) rule did NOT assess them — an intentional public/reference table (a catalog) and a genuine cross-user leak look identical here, and only a declared tenant key would let the rule tell them apart. Named so the sparing can be checked rather than read as clean from the absence of a finding: plans (plans_select_public); support_categories (support_categories_select_all); billing_products (billing_products_read_all); billing_prices (billing_prices_read_all).
findings.impact: This is an assumption disclosure, not a defect. A spared USING(true) may be a correct world-readable catalog OR a reference-shaped table that is actually leaking rows across users — the static review cannot decide without a tenant key, and silence here is not evidence of safety.
findings.fix: Confirm each table above is intentionally world-readable (a published catalog/reference list). If it is really tenant- or owner-scoped under a column the review did not recognise, re-run with `--tenant-key <column>` so the USING(true) rule assesses it instead of sparing it.

findings.title: SECURITY DEFINER public.promote_to_admin — caller-authorization review
findings.impact: A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with the owner's privileges — without a caller check, any exposed role can invoke it to escalate (e.g. self-promote to admin) or write outside its own tenant.
findings.fix: Add an explicit caller-authorization guard (verify auth.uid() owns the row or holds the required role) before the privileged write, or REVOKE EXECUTE from anon/authenticated.
findings.okWhen: The body checks the caller's identity/role/tenant before the write, or the write isn't actually privileged.
findings.notOkWhen: Any exposed caller can trigger the privileged write without the function verifying who they are.

findings.title: SECURITY DEFINER public.get_user_by_email is granted to anon and reads data with no caller check
findings.evidence: public.get_user_by_email is SECURITY DEFINER (runs as owner, bypasses RLS), returns/reads data, has no auth.uid()/auth.jwt() caller check, and is EXPLICITLY granted execute to the anon/public role. An unauthenticated caller can invoke it to enumerate or dump data across every tenant.
findings.impact: A SECURITY DEFINER reader reachable by anon runs with the owner's privileges and no RLS — anyone holding the anon key can dump or enumerate the data it returns for any tenant.
findings.fix: REVOKE EXECUTE … FROM anon (and public), or add a caller-authorization check (auth.uid()/role/tenant) inside the function before it returns data. Grant only to the specific authenticated role that needs it, if any.
cwe: CWE-269: Improper Privilege Management

findings.title: Function public.search_tickets_unsafe builds dynamic SQL by concatenating a parameter (SQL injection)
findings.evidence: EXECUTE in public.search_tickets_unsafe splices the parameter(s) p_query into the dynamic query by string concatenation (|| / format %s) with no quote_literal/quote_ident/%L/%I escaping — and the function is SECURITY DEFINER, so the injected query runs as the owner, bypassing RLS. CWE-89.
findings.impact: A caller controls the SQL text: they can read, modify, or drop any data the function's role can reach (for a SECURITY DEFINER function, that is the table owner's full access, bypassing RLS).
findings.fix: Never concatenate a parameter into EXECUTE. Use parameterized dynamic SQL (`EXECUTE '… where col = $1' USING p`), or quote_literal()/quote_ident() / format() with %L/%I for identifiers and literals.
cwe: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

findings.title: RLS policy profiles_select_self re-evaluates auth.* per row
findings.evidence: Policy profiles_select_self on public.profiles calls auth.uid() in USING without a (select …) wrapper, so Postgres re-evaluates it once per candidate row instead of once per query — Supabase's auth_rls_initplan advisor lint, read here from migration SQL.
findings.impact: Every query the policy guards pays the auth function call per row scanned — linear slowdown that grows with table size and is invisible until the table does.
findings.fix: Wrap the call in a subquery — e.g. auth.uid() → (select auth.uid()) — to hoist it to a once-per-query initplan. Verify the rewritten policy is behavior-identical before shipping. Confirm against the live advisor (pnpm perf-scan).

findings.title: Storage bucket "kyc-documents" is created public in migration SQL
findings.taxonomy: Public storage bucket declared in migration SQL (static)
findings.evidence: insert into storage.buckets sets public = true for "kyc-documents" in supabase/migrations/20260727000001_storage_buckets_static.sql. Supabase serves every object in a public bucket unauthenticated from /storage/v1/object/public/kyc-documents/<path>; storage.objects RLS policies do not apply to that path.
findings.impact: Anyone who learns or guesses an object path reads it — no session, no policy evaluation. If "kyc-documents" holds user uploads (documents, identity scans, invoices) rather than public assets, every tenant's files are world-readable by URL.
findings.fix: Set public = false for "kyc-documents" and serve its objects through signed URLs, plus a storage.objects SELECT policy scoping objects to their owner/tenant. Leave it public only if the bucket holds assets that are meant to be served to anonymous visitors.
cwe: CWE-668: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere

findings.title: storage.objects policy exports_read_anon grants anonymous read with no owner predicate
findings.taxonomy: storage.objects read policy open to anon (static)
findings.evidence: Policy exports_read_anon is FOR SELECT TO anon with USING (bucket_id = 'exports') — the clause narrows the bucket but never references the caller (auth.uid()/auth.jwt()/owner), so every object it covers is readable by an unauthenticated holder of the anon key.
findings.impact: Storage is a separate door onto tenant data. A private bucket whose SELECT policy is open to anon leaks every object in it — the PostgREST/RLS results say nothing about this surface.
findings.fix: Scope the policy to the object's owner or tenant (e.g. USING (bucket_id = '…' and (storage.foldername(name))[1] = auth.uid()::text)), or grant it TO authenticated only if every signed-in user is genuinely entitled to every object.
cwe: CWE-668: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere

findings.taxonomy: Coverage — SQL outside the schema surfaces M1 reads
findings.evidence: M1's static SQL pass reads two surfaces: every `supabase/migrations/*.sql` and a root `schema.sql`. 2 other .sql file(s) are present and were NOT read: public/backup.sql, supabase/seed.sql. The RLS-enablement, policy-semantics, SECURITY DEFINER, dynamic-SQL and storage-bucket checks therefore never saw whatever they contain.
findings.impact: If any of these files is where the schema actually lives, every static SQL finding in this report is drawn from an incomplete picture — a permissive policy or a public storage bucket declared only there was never assessed. Counted and named here so their absence cannot be read as a clean result.
findings.fix: If one of these files is the schema, move it to `supabase/migrations/` or a root `schema.sql` (the two layouts Harvey reads) — or say which one it is so the scan can be pointed at it. findings.title: Open signup enabled ([auth] enable_signup = true)
findings.evidence: [auth] sets enable_signup = true — anyone can self-register an account without an invite.
findings.impact: Any anonymous visitor can create an account, enabling mass fake-account signup and abuse of any per-account resource.
findings.fix: Set enable_signup = false and provision users via invite/admin, unless open self-registration is a deliberate product decision with abuse controls.
cwe: CWE-287: Improper Authentication

findings.title: Email confirmation disabled ([auth.email] enable_confirmations = false)
findings.evidence: [auth.email] sets enable_confirmations = false — accounts authenticate without proving ownership of the email address.
findings.impact: Signups are effectively auto-confirmed: an attacker can register accounts against emails they do not control (mass fake-account signup, account-takeover setups). The static twin of the live mailer_autoconfirm=true check.
findings.fix: Set enable_confirmations = true so a signup must confirm the email before the account is usable.
cwe: CWE-287: Improper Authentication

findings.title: Browser extension Session Sync Helper requests broad host access with a sensitive capability
findings.evidence: manifest.json (v3) declares broad host access (https://*/*) together with the sensitive capability(ies) cookies. With a broad host + cookies, the extension can read auth/session cookies on EVERY site the user visits, not only the origin it needs.
findings.impact: A broad host pattern plus cookies/webRequest/tabs lets the extension read session tokens, intercept requests, or enumerate tabs/history across all of the user's browsing — far beyond the single origin it operates on. If the extension (or an update) is compromised, every site's session is exposed.
findings.fix: Scope host_permissions/content_scripts.matches to the specific origin(s) the extension needs (e.g. https://app.example.com/*), and request only the capabilities that origin requires. Use activeTab / optional_permissions requested at runtime instead of a broad standing grant.
cwe: CWE-250: Execution with Unnecessary Privileges

findings.title: Tenant isolation not assessed in Python/Go/Rust/C# source
findings.taxonomy: Coverage — non-JS/TS source not analysed for tenant isolation
findings.evidence: Source files in languages M1 cannot analyse were found in the target: Python (4 files, e.g. src/m5-polyglot/python-negative.py); Go (2 files, e.g. src/m5-polyglot/library-positive.go); Rust (2 files, e.g. src/m5-polyglot/rust-negative.rs); C# (1 file, e.g. src/m5-polyglot/unsupported.cs). Harvey's tenant-isolation rules are JavaScript/TypeScript-only (every custom semgrep rule declares `languages: [javascript, typescript]`, and the tenant-scope AST detectors parse TypeScript). The third-party packs Harvey also runs (p/owasp-top-ten, p/secrets, p/security-audit) cover some of these languages for generic issues, but none of them is tenant-isolation aware.
findings.impact: A service in one of these languages that queries the same tables bypasses RLS with exactly the same effect as a broken policy — and it was NOT assessed for tenant scoping. Recorded so the absence of M1 findings for this code reads as 'not assessed', not 'assessed and clean'.
findings.fix: Review data access in these files by hand: every query must filter on the tenant/owner column, and any service-role/superuser database credential used from them must not be reachable by user input.

findings.title: .github/workflows/saml-integration-test.yml declares no GITHUB_TOKEN permissions
findings.taxonomy: GitHub Actions workflow declares no token permissions
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/saml-integration-test.yml defines jobs but has no `permissions:` block at workflow or job level, so GITHUB_TOKEN inherits the repository's DEFAULT workflow permissions. That default is a repository/organisation setting this scan cannot read.
findings.impact: Where the default is still 'Read and write' — GitHub's setting for repositories created before February 2023, and for any organisation that has not changed it — every job in this workflow runs with a token that can push commits, publish packages and edit pull requests, whether or not it needs to.
findings.fix: Add an explicit least-privilege block (`permissions: { contents: read }`) at the top of the workflow and widen it per job where a job genuinely writes. Independently, set the repository/organisation default workflow permissions to read-only.
cwe: CWE-732: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource

findings.title: .github/workflows/token-job-write-all.yml grants GITHUB_TOKEN write-all
findings.taxonomy: GitHub Actions workflow grants write-all token permissions
findings.evidence: `permissions: write-all` is declared for a job in .github/workflows/token-job-write-all.yml, giving GITHUB_TOKEN every scope GitHub offers — contents, packages, deployments, id-token, and write access to issues, pull requests and actions.
findings.impact: Any code that runs in this workflow — a build script, a third-party action, an injected string from a pull-request title — acts with full write access to the repository. Combined with a pull_request_target trigger that checks out the PR head, this is the standard path from an untrusted PR to a repository takeover.
findings.fix: Replace write-all with the narrowest block the jobs actually need (`permissions: { contents: read }` at the top of the workflow, widened per job only where a job genuinely writes). Set the repository default workflow permissions to read-only so an omitted block is safe too.

findings.title: Hallucinated-dependency (slopsquat) existence check did not run for 11 dependencies
findings.taxonomy: Coverage — npm-registry existence check not assessed

findings.title: Dependency "@img/sharp-libvips-linux-riscv64@1.2.4" is licensed LGPL-3.0-or-later — possible copyleft conflict
findings.evidence: the lockfile reports "@img/sharp-libvips-linux-riscv64@1.2.4" under "LGPL-3.0-or-later" (SPDX), a strong-copyleft license. This package is reached only through the resolved dependency tree.
findings.impact: Strong-copyleft licenses (GPL/AGPL/LGPL and similar) impose reciprocal source-disclosure obligations that typically conflict with a closed/proprietary distribution — this needs a legal review before shipping, not just a code fix.
findings.fix: Confirm the actual distribution/linking model with counsel, or replace "@img/sharp-libvips-linux-riscv64" with a permissively-licensed alternative.

findings.title: Dependency "caniuse-lite@1.0.30001803" has no clear license — review

findings.impact: A dependency with no confirmed license (missing, ambiguous, or npm's UNLICENSED marker) carries no confirmed grant to use, modify, or redistribute it — a legal exposure in a distributed/commercial product, distinct from a security bug.
findings.fix: Confirm "caniuse-lite"'s actual license (its repository/README, or the maintainer directly) and record the finding; replace it if no usable license exists.

findings.title: Dependency license-compliance check did not run for 10 packages
findings.evidence: License scope: 400 packages (11 declared in a manifest, 389 reached only through the resolved tree) from package-lock.json. The declared half was read from 1 manifest (no workspace globs declared). The dependency license lookup could not reach a verdict: the live npm-registry fallback was deliberately skipped for this pass (skipNetworkChecks), so packages whose license the lockfile does not record could not be classified. Not assessed: expres, left-pad, react-supabase-helpers, busboy@1.6.0, console-browserify@1.2.0, crossenv@0.0.0-synthetic, enhanced-resolve@4.5.0, querystring-es3@0.2.1, streamsearch@1.1.0, uid@0.0.0-synthetic.
findings.impact: License classification reads the license the lockfile or the registry records; without it no copyleft or unlicensed dependency can be identified. The absence of license findings for these packages is a disclosed coverage gap, NOT a clean license bill.
findings.fix: Re-run the scan from a machine with direct access to https://registry.npmjs.org (no proxy interception, no rate limit in effect) so this tier reports a verdict instead of a coverage gap.

findings.title: Supply-chain scope: 4 resolved-tree check families; declaration ranges assessed separately
findings.evidence: Declared set: 11 package names from 1 manifest (no workspace globs declared). Resolved tree: 365 package names from package-lock.json. Read the whole resolved tree: SUP-TYPO-* (typosquat); SUP-IOC-* (known-malicious names); SUP-LICENSE-* (license compliance); SUP-INSTALL-SCRIPT-DEP (a RESOLVED package's own install-time lifecycle script, transitive ones included), because package-lock.json v2/v3 records `hasInstallScript` per resolved entry (#1351). Limited to the declared manifests: SUP-SLOPSQUAT-* over 11 declared names, because a package the lockfile resolved carries an integrity hash against a published tarball and has by construction been published — a registry HEAD over the transitive tree would spend thousands of live requests confirming what the lockfile already proves; DEP-CVE-* (the curated offline CVE table), because osv-scanner walked the whole lockfile this pass and widening the curated table would double-report its rows. SUP-UNPINNED and SUP-NON-REGISTRY examine 11 manifest declarations plus admitted npm v2/v3 dependency/devDependency/optionalDependency edges. package-lock.json (package-lock version 3, read): 725 admitted third-party range edges, 725 input unit(s) examined, 0 present/unread unit(s), 0 unsupported source schema(s). Excluded copies/constraints: root 8, workspace 0, link 0, peer 12. Read npm v2/v3 third-party dependency, devDependency and optionalDependency declarations. Root/workspace/link copies are excluded because manifests are authoritative; peer ranges are intentionally excluded compatibility constraints. Falsifier for an unread-format limit: a parser/registry replay of the named file that emits validated owner-path declaration edges and reports zero unread/unsupported units. Peer ranges are intentionally excluded compatibility constraints; the peer-only control in src/scan/mechanical.test.ts guards that boundary.
findings.impact: A manifest-scoped check cannot see a package reached only through the resolved dependency tree. The absence of its findings across that tree is a disclosed scope boundary, NOT a verdict that the tree is clean.
findings.fix: Keep root/workspace manifests authoritative and enforce a committed lockfile with frozen installs. npm v2/v3 declaration ranges are assessed; unread, unsupported or malformed range sources above need a validated format-specific parser/consumer before their absence of findings can count as coverage. For third-party declarations, update or override the owning dependency rather than editing generated lock metadata. Declare every workspace member so its manifest is included.

findings.taxonomy: In-memory rate limiter (per-instance, resets on cold start)

findings.impact: Each serverless instance keeps its own counter and every cold start resets it, so the real budget is the limit times the number of live instances — and an attacker who paces requests never hits it at all.
findings.fix: Move the counter to a store shared across instances (Redis/Upstash, Vercel KV, or a database row with an atomic increment).

findings.title: src/components/AdminGateStorage.tsx — authorization decision enforced in client code (bypassable)
findings.evidence: Heuristic "client-side-authz" matched in src/components/AdminGateStorage.tsx.
findings.impact: The role/privilege check runs in the browser, where the user controls Web Storage and the JS bundle — they can flip the gate open (edit storage, patch the bundle) and reach the privileged view/action. Any data the gate is supposed to protect is already in the client.

findings.title: src/owasp-mt/rate-limit-not-per-tenant.ts rate-limits with process-local state, which does not limit on a serverless host
findings.taxonomy: In-memory rate limiter (per-instance, resets on cold start)
findings.evidence: Rate-limit intent plus a module-scope Map/Set/object counter store, and no shared-store (Redis/KV/DB) hint anywhere in src/owasp-mt/rate-limit-not-per-tenant.ts.
findings.impact: Each serverless instance keeps its own counter and every cold start resets it, so the real budget is the limit times the number of live instances — and an attacker who paces requests never hits it at all.
findings.fix: Move the counter to a store shared across instances (Redis/Upstash, Vercel KV, or a database row with an atomic increment).

findings.title: pages/api/billing/invoice.js — authenticated handler queries rows scoped by a client-supplied `tenant_id`
findings.taxonomy: Object-level authorization gap: client-supplied owner id scopes the query
findings.evidence: Heuristic "bola-body-owner": the handler authenticates the caller (binding `session`) yet scopes its service-role query with `.eq("tenant_id", …)` on a value rooted in the request object, with no comparison against `session` in the body.
findings.impact: The caller is authenticated but never authorized for the object: any signed-in user can put another tenant's/user's id in the request and read (or write) that tenant's rows — the service-role client bypasses RLS, so this scoping is the only gate.
findings.fix: Scope the query to the verified session (e.g. `.eq("tenant_id", session.user.tenantId)`), or explicitly compare the request's id against the session's and reject mismatches.
cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

findings.title: Request-controlled URL reaches `downloadRemote()`, a cross-file fetch wrapper
findings.taxonomy: M1 — SSRF via an uncurated cross-file fetch wrapper
findings.evidence: `downloadRemote` is imported from lib/dl-fetch.ts, where its only use of its parameter `target` is passing it straight to a fetch-family call — a thin pass-through with no host check. Here it is called with `new URL(req.url).searchParams.get("url") || ""`, a request-derived value.
findings.impact: SSRF: the server can be made to fetch an attacker-chosen URL, reaching internal services or cloud metadata endpoints depending on the deploy network.
findings.fix: Validate the host against an allowlist and block internal/link-local ranges before the value reaches the wrapper, or add that check inside the wrapper itself.
cwe: CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)

findings.title: lib/express-pg-idor.js — authenticated handler passes a client-supplied id straight into findOrderById(...)

findings.title: lib/express-pg-resjson-direct.js — res.json(...) names the curated-sensitive field "passwordHash" as a direct property of the object it returns

findings.title: src/db/task-repo.ts — `prisma.task.findUnique` filters by `id` alone, with no tenant/owner scope
findings.taxonomy: Object-level authorization gap: Prisma query filtered by primary key with no tenant scope
findings.evidence: Heuristic "prisma-tenant-scope": `prisma.task.findUnique({ where: { id, … } })` filters by the primary key alone — no tenant/owner column (organizationId/tenantId/teamId/userId/…) appears anywhere in the where clause.
findings.impact: A Prisma app has no database-level tenant enforcement (no RLS), so this query's where clause is the only isolation gate. Filtered by id alone, any authenticated user who substitutes another tenant's id reads or mutates that tenant's row — the cross-tenant BOLA/IDOR that made proposit Critical.
findings.fix: Add the caller's tenant/owner to the filter (e.g. `where: { id, organizationId }` scoped from the verified session), or compare the fetched row's owner against the session and reject a mismatch before returning/mutating it. Prefer `findFirst`/`updateMany`/`deleteMany` for a non-unique tenant predicate.
cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

findings.title: pages/api/billing/invoice.js — tenant scope `tenant_id` is populated from the request (`req.body.tenantId`)
findings.taxonomy: Object-level authorization gap: tenant predicate populated from the request
findings.evidence: Heuristic "client-supplied-tenant": `.eq("tenant_id", …)` scopes on `tenant_id`, and that value traces to `req.body.tenantId` through same-function assignments. The query carries a tenant predicate and looks correctly scoped; the caller chooses which tenant it selects.
findings.impact: The tenant discriminator is attacker-controlled, so the isolation gate is set by the request it is supposed to constrain: any authenticated caller reads or mutates another tenant's rows by editing one field. Because the predicate is present and names the right column, this passes code review and every detector that checks whether a tenant filter exists.
findings.fix: Derive `tenant_id` from the verified session on the server (`session.user.tenant_id` / the JWT claim), never from the request. If the caller must name a tenant — a multi-tenant admin or account switcher — compare the supplied value against the session's tenant membership and reject a mismatch before the query runs.
cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

findings.impact: The tenant discriminator is attacker-controlled, so the isolation gate is set by the request it is supposed to constrain: any authenticated caller reads or mutates another tenant's rows by editing one field. Because the predicate is present and names the right column, this passes code review and every detector that checks whether a tenant filter exists.
findings.fix: Derive `tenant_id` from the verified session on the server (`session.user.tenant_id` / the JWT claim), never from the request. If the caller must name a tenant — a multi-tenant admin or account switcher — compare the supplied value against the session's tenant membership and reject a mismatch before the query runs.
cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

findings.title: src/owasp-mt/tenant-guc-session-scoped.ts:13 — tenant GUC set with SET, not SET LOCAL
findings.taxonomy: Tenant GUC set with SET rather than SET LOCAL, leaking across a pooled connection
findings.evidence: Heuristic "tenant-guc-scope" matched `SET app.current_tenant =` in a query call in src/owasp-mt/tenant-guc-session-scoped.ts:13. No LOCAL / third `true` argument was found on the same line.
findings.impact: Under transaction-mode pooling this setting outlives the transaction and stays on the connection when it returns to the pool, so the next request to borrow that connection is evaluated against the PREVIOUS tenant's identifier — a cross-tenant read that leaves the RLS policy, schema and application code all looking correct.
findings.fix: Use `SET LOCAL <guc> = …` or `set_config('<guc>', …, true)` so the setting is scoped to the current transaction and cannot outlive it in the pool.
cwe: CWE-668: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere

findings.title: src/owasp-mt/cache-key-no-tenant.ts — cache key has no tenant discriminator, though `tenantId` is in scope
findings.taxonomy: Cache key without a tenant discriminator (cross-tenant cache poisoning)
findings.evidence: Heuristic "cache-tenant-scope" matched a .get/.set read-through cache pair keyed on ``dashboard:${boardId}``, which does not mention the in-scope tenant parameter `tenantId`.
findings.impact: The first tenant to populate this cache entry serves its rows to every other tenant that requests the same resource id — OWASP's 'Shared Resource Poisoning' risk.
findings.fix: Prefix the cache key with the tenant discriminator, e.g. `t:${tenantId}:...`, or use a per-tenant cache namespace.
cwe: CWE-668: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere

findings.title: 1 cache site not judged for tenant scoping
findings.taxonomy: Coverage — cache sites outside the tenant-scope heuristic's bounds
findings.evidence: The cache-tenant-scope heuristic (CACHE-key-no-tenant) judged neither of these classes. 1 read-through cache get/set pair sit in a function with no tenant/org/workspace-named identifier in scope — as a parameter, a local binding, or a property such as `session.tenantId` — so the heuristic cannot tell an intentionally global cache from one whose tenant context is reached through a name it does not recognise. 0 cache writes have no paired read on the same key, which #1196 deliberately leaves alone as a weaker signal.

findings.title: pages/api/upload-safe.js — storage upload() path has no tenant prefix or ownership check
findings.taxonomy: Storage object path without a tenant prefix (cross-tenant object read/overwrite)
findings.evidence: Heuristic "storage-tenant-scope" matched `storage.from(...).upload(req.query.name, …)`, whose path does not mention a tenant/org discriminator or a session accessor.
findings.impact: In a shared bucket, one tenant can overwrite or read another tenant's object by supplying the same filename — the path is the only isolation gate and it carries no tenant scope.

findings.title: src/owasp-mt/audit-log-no-tenant.ts — audit log entry records the actor but no tenant
findings.taxonomy: Audit log entry without a tenant discriminator
findings.evidence: Heuristic "audit-log-tenant" matched a `logger` entry that names the actor `userId` and a state change, with no tenant/organisation/workspace discriminator in its arguments. Assumes a multi-tenant target and a sink that does not inject the tenant upstream — a bound child logger is invisible to a static pass, so confirm before acting.
findings.impact: A cross-tenant access cannot be reconstructed or alerted on after the fact: the trail records who and what, but not which tenant's data was touched, so entries cannot be grouped or scoped per tenant during an investigation.

findings.title: src/d091/dropped-column-reader.ts — reads `d091_quotes.legacy_grade`, a column the migrations already removed

findings.impact: The query fails at runtime the first time this path is exercised. Column names are strings inside the query chain, so the type checker cannot see the break and happy-path tests written against the new schema still pass — the contract migration shipped before the readers were switched over.

findings.title: src/d091/batch-send-claim.ts — batch job stamps the row after sending, not before
findings.taxonomy: Batch send stamped after dispatch instead of claimed before
findings.evidence: Heuristic "claim-before-send" matched `sendReminder(…)` inside a loop, followed by an `.update()` setting a sent-style timestamp on `d091_reminders` — the row is marked sent only after the send returns.
findings.impact: A retry, or a second overlapping run of the same job, re-sends every row whose stamp had not yet landed. A single-run test passes: the double send needs a crash inside the send window or two concurrent runs.
findings.fix: CAS-claim the row before sending — `.update({ sent_at: … }).is('sent_at', null).select('id')` — and skip the send when zero rows were claimed.
cwe: CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization ('Race Condition')

findings.title: src/d091/webhook-dedup-order.ts — idempotency row written before the handler it guards
findings.taxonomy: Idempotency row written before the dispatched handler
findings.evidence: Heuristic "dedup-before-dispatch" matched an insert into `d091_webhook_events` followed by `handleSubscriptionEvent(…)` — the dedup row lands before the work it guards runs.
findings.impact: A crash between the insert and the handler makes the provider's genuine retry look like a duplicate, so the work never completes and nothing reports it: the row says 'processed' when it means 'received'.
findings.fix: Write the idempotency row AFTER the dispatched handler completes, so its existence means 'fully processed'. Track in-flight work with a separate `processing_started_at` if reconciliation needs it.
cwe: CWE-754: Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions

findings.title: src/d091/webhook-ordering.ts — webhook state applied with no ordering guard
findings.taxonomy: Webhook state applied without an ordering guard
findings.evidence: Heuristic "webhook-ordering" matched a handler whose event parameter `event` carries the ordering field `created`, writing event-derived state into `d091_subscriptions`, with no comparison against a stored last-applied value anywhere in this function. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK: it reads THIS FUNCTION BODY only, with NO webhook-path prefilter. A comparison performed inside a wrapper in another module, a database trigger, or a conditional `WHERE created > …` built elsewhere is OUTSIDE what this pass can see. FIELD PRECISION IS UNMEASURED: MEASURED 2026-08-15 with `pnpm corpus-drift --install --shard N/3 --json corpus-drift-shardN.json --baseline-findings prior-drift/corpus-drift.json` for N=1,2,3 in Actions run 31873008063, the production `idempotency` registry ledger examined 13,104 source units across 17 pinned targets and emitted ZERO findings (merged artifact SHA-256 `5eaeb965920aacf2e83c1f78def674691b2f214935990d8ffb85b3d7f73311ff`). Zero firings leave the false-positive rate undefined — treat this as a prompt to check, not as a confirmed defect.
findings.impact: Under at-least-once, unordered delivery a stale event arriving after a fresher one overwrites newer state — a cancelled subscription reactivated by a late `updated` delivery, a downgraded plan restored. Replay dedup does not prevent it: the two deliveries are genuinely different events.
findings.fix: Compare the event's `created` against the last-applied value on the row and skip the write when it is not newer — a conditional update (`... .gt("created", stored)`, or `WHERE created < $new`) keeps the check atomic with the write.
cwe: CWE-841: Improper Enforcement of Behavioral Workflow

findings.title: src/inngest/external-send-idempotency-headers-override-malformed.ts — idempotency key does not identify one stable scoped operation
findings.taxonomy: Idempotency key does not identify a stable scoped operation
findings.evidence: Heuristic "external-send-idempotency-key" classified the https://api.resend.com key as clock-or-attempt-derived: `Date.now().toString()` depends on time or attempt-local state, so a retry changes the key. PROVIDER COLLISION DOMAIN: resend. LOGICAL OPERATION: POST /emails. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK: it reads exact provider slots and immutable provenance in THIS FILE only, then compares proven contracts across ALL ADMITTED PROJECT FILES. FALSIFIER: evaluate the key for two retry attempts of the same logical operation and show byte-for-byte equality.
findings.impact: If a retry changes the key, the provider performs the logical operation twice. If different tenant/entity/operation tuples share the key, the provider suppresses legitimate work as a duplicate.
findings.fix: Derive the key from the domain's immutable tenant/entity/operation identity so identical logical operations reproduce one key and different scoped operations cannot collide. Payload hashing is optional, not a universal requirement.

findings.title: src/d091/budget-gate-stale.ts — allowance `budget` read once, then consumed across a loop without re-reading
findings.taxonomy: Quota gate consumed across a loop without re-reading
findings.evidence: Heuristic "stale-quota-read" matched `budget`, bound from `supabase .from("d091_budgets") .select("remaining_cents") .eq("tenant_id", tenantId) .single()`, compared inside a loop whose body awaits work and contains no re-read of that value.
findings.impact: From the second iteration on, the cap is enforced against a value that stopped being true. Two overlapping runs, or a long enough batch, overrun the budget without any error — sequential single-run tests pass because a single iteration is always within the cap.
findings.fix: Re-read the allowance between consuming operations, or make the gate atomic at the database level — an advisory lock, or a transactional reserve-row that debits the allowance in the same statement that checks it.
cwe: CWE-367: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition

findings.title: jobs.emit("error", ...) has no same-file error listener
findings.taxonomy: EventEmitter emits 'error' with no registered listener
findings.evidence: `jobs.emit("error", new Error(`job ${id} failed`))` — no `jobs.on("error", ...)`/`.once("error", ...)` anywhere else in src/owasp-node/unhandled-rejection.ts.
findings.impact: Node re-throws an 'error' event with no listener, crashing the process — a remote denial of service if the emit is reachable from a request.
findings.fix: Register an error listener on jobs (`jobs.on("error", (err) => { ... })`) before it can emit, or bind `process.on("uncaughtException", ...)` as a last-resort backstop.
cwe: CWE-248: Uncaught Exception

findings.title: Express app never disables the X-Powered-By response header
findings.evidence: `express()` builds an Express app, and no `disable("x-powered-by")`, `set("x-powered-by", false)`, `removeHeader("X-Powered-By")` or helmet use appears anywhere in lib/express-cors-nocreds.js — Express therefore sets `X-Powered-By: Express` on every response this app serves. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK: it reads the module that CONSTRUCTS the app and nothing else. A disable applied in another module that imports this app, or a header stripped at a reverse proxy, CDN or ingress in front of it, is OUTSIDE what this pass can see — so a live response may well not carry the header. Confirm against the deployed response before treating this as present.
findings.impact: Every response names the server framework, which lets an attacker skip fingerprinting and go straight to Express- and middleware-specific exploits when a CVE lands. Low on its own; it is reconnaissance that shortens the path to a real finding.
findings.fix: Call `app.disable("x-powered-by")` immediately after creating the app (or mount `helmet()`, whose hidePoweredBy default removes it). If the header is already stripped at a proxy or CDN, keep the app-level disable anyway so the app is not dependent on the edge staying configured.
cwe: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor

findings.title: Express app sets no security response headers
findings.taxonomy: Express app sets no security response headers
findings.evidence: `express()` builds an Express app, and no Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options or Content-Security-Policy is set anywhere in lib/express-cors-nocreds.js — by any means, including a header middleware. SCOPE OF THIS CHECK: it reads the module that CONSTRUCTS the app and nothing else. Headers applied by a middleware module this pass did not read, or added at a reverse proxy, CDN or ingress in front of the app, are OUTSIDE what it can see — so a live response may well carry them. Confirm against the deployed response before treating these as absent. Note this is a check on the RESPONSE HEADERS, not on which package sets them: an app that sets them by hand clears it exactly as one mounting a header middleware does.
findings.impact: Without HSTS a downgraded request can be intercepted over plain HTTP; without X-Frame-Options or a frame-ancestors directive the pages can be framed for clickjacking; without nosniff a browser may MIME-sniff a response into an executable content type. These are the browser-side defences that cost nothing to set and are absent by default in Express, which sets no security headers of its own.
findings.fix: Set the headers once, at the top of the app — either by hand in a small middleware (`res.setHeader("Strict-Transport-Security", …)`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, and a Content-Security-Policy) or with a header middleware, whichever fits the codebase. If they are already added at a proxy or CDN, setting them in the app too keeps it from depending on the edge staying configured.
cwe: CWE-693: Protection Mechanism Failure

findings.title: req.on("data", ...) accumulates the request body with no size limit
findings.taxonomy: Request body accumulated with no size limit
findings.evidence: `req.on("data", (c: Buffer) => chunks.push(c))` buffers each chunk, and no byte ceiling — no running-total comparison, no `req.destroy()`/`.pause()`, no limit/max value — appears anywhere in the enclosing handler in src/owasp-node/no-request-size-limit.ts. A ceiling imposed by middleware, a wrapper in another module, or a reverse proxy is OUTSIDE what this pass reads.
findings.impact: One request with an arbitrarily large body is buffered whole in memory, so a single caller can exhaust the process heap — a denial of service that needs no authentication.
findings.fix: Track the accumulated byte count and reject past a ceiling sized to what the route legitimately needs (`if (received > MAX_BYTES) { req.destroy(); return; }`), or read the body through a bounded parser (express.json({ limit: "100kb" }), raw-body's `limit` option).
cwe: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

findings.title: src/owasp-react/ssr-browser-sanitizer.tsx — browser-only sanitizer runs on the server
findings.taxonomy: Browser-only sanitizer in a server-rendered component
findings.evidence: `DOMPurify.sanitize(article.body)` — `dompurify` is imported here and `ArticleBody` is an async component — React has no async Client Components, so it renders on the server. DOMPurify depends on browser DOM APIs it does not have in Node.
findings.impact: The sanitizer call reads as protection to reviewers and to every dangerouslySetInnerHTML rule (all of them exclude an import-bound sanitizer wrap), but on the server it throws or returns the input unchanged. The raw HTML renders during SSR — before hydration, and before any client-side guard can run.
findings.fix: Swap `dompurify` for a server-compatible sanitizer (`isomorphic-dompurify` or `sanitize-html`), or construct DOMPurify against a supplied DOM (`createDOMPurify(new JSDOM('').window)`).
cwe: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

findings.title: src/owasp-react/oversharing-props-spread.tsx — whole object passed as a prop carries sensitive fields
findings.evidence: `<Avatar {...account} />` hands `Avatar` the whole `account`, whose declared type carries `passwordHash`.
findings.impact: Every field of the object reaches React's Fiber tree and the serialized props of any SSR payload, whether or not the component renders it — readable by browser extensions, React DevTools and session-recording scripts. SCOPE: the type must be declared in the same file (an imported one is not resolved), only declared types are read, and the sensitive-name list is fixed, so an app's own vocabulary for a sensitive field is not recognised.
findings.fix: Pass only the fields `Avatar` renders (`const { … } = account`), or project the object into a view model before it crosses the component boundary.
cwe: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
